title: The four senses of scripture (CCC 115–119)
hook: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical: one text, many depths

segments.voice: Yesterday, apostolic succession: a teaching handed on, hand to hand. Your line was an unbroken line. What did you pass on? Today, how the Church reads what was handed on. Day one thousand sixty-six.

On a piano stand, a sheet of music lies open. A beginner reads the notes, one at a time, and gets them right. A teacher, reading the same page, hears the harmony moving underneath. The composer sees where the whole piece is heading, pages ahead. Nobody has changed a single note. The depth of the reading is what changed. The Catholic tradition reads scripture a little like that: the same verse, read on several levels at once. Today's word: the four senses.
screen: `THE BEGINNER READS THE NOTES.` → `THE TEACHER HEARS THE HARMONY.` → `SAME PAGE, DEEPER READING.`

segments.voice: The Catechism starts with two senses of scripture: the literal and the spiritual. Then it divides the spiritual into three. So, four in all: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. First, and underneath everything, the literal: what the words actually say, what the writer meant. The Catechism, following Thomas Aquinas, says every other sense is built on this one. Then the allegorical: how the events point to Christ. Paul uses the very word. In Galatians, writing about Abraham's two sons, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Which things are said by an allegory." Then the moral: what the text asks of how we live. Paul again, about Israel in the desert: these things "are written for our correction." Then the anagogical: where it all leads in the end, toward the life of heaven. The Catechism's own example of the allegorical sense is the crossing of the Red Sea, a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian baptism. Some readers run that same story through all four. Literally, Israel walks through the sea and out of slavery. Allegorically, Christ's victory, and baptism. Morally, leaving behind what holds a person captive. Anagogically, the last crossing, into the promised land. The Catechism also quotes a medieval rhyme that packs it into a pocket. The letter teaches what happened. Allegory, what to believe. The moral sense, what to do. Anagogy, where you're heading. The point isn't a secret code. The literal comes first, and the other senses grow out of it, not away from it. That's the carry: one text, four depths. The page stays the same. The reading goes deeper.
screen: `LITERAL FIRST, UNDER EVERYTHING.` · `ALLEGORICAL, MORAL, ANAGOGICAL.` · `THE RED SEA, FOUR WAYS.` · `WHAT HAPPENED, BELIEVE, DO, HEADING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a verse four ways. Take this line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." Settle, and breathe. Say it once, slowly. Then ask four questions, with a breath between each. What happened? Pilgrims setting off for the temple in Jerusalem. What might it show about Christ? What does it ask of me today? And where is it heading, in the end? Don't hurry. Some questions may stay unanswered; that's fine. If you pray, you can say the line again as your own. The bell holds the time.
Four senses. Literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical: one text read at four depths, with the literal underneath them all. Today's word.
Your line: one text, four depths. Today, take one line you read, a verse, a poem, a note from a friend, and look for a second layer under the first. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic preachers and readers draw on the four senses when they explain scripture, and the Church's liturgy often pairs an Old Testament story with a Gospel reading so that one sheds light on the other.

fork.setup: Israel walks through the sea and out of Egypt. the Catechism gives an allegorical reading of it. which one?
options: a lesson in courage under pressure
a sign of Christ's victory and of baptism
fork.reveal: the Catechism's allegorical example is the Red Sea crossing as a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian baptism. courage would be a moral reading; heaven, an anagogical one.

original.note: Greek, from Galatians 4:24: things spoken as an allegory. Paul's own word.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading the Bible for hidden codes.
what it means: one text at four depths: what happened, what it shows of Christ, how to live, and where it leads.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism's two senses, literal and spiritual, the spiritual in three; Aquinas on the literal as foundation; the medieval rhyme beginning 'littera gesta docet'.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Galatians 4:24, 1 Corinthians 10:11 ('are written for our correction') and Psalm 121:1.

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): the two senses and three spiritual senses CCC 115; literal as foundation, citing Aquinas, CCC 116; the Red Sea as allegorical example CCC 117; the medieval couplet CCC 118 (paraphrased in English).

The four-way reading of the Red Sea beyond the allegorical sense is offered as what 'some readers' do; it is not the Catechism's own example for the moral and anagogical senses (CCC 117 uses other examples). Keeper may prefer the Catechism's examples.
